clue.text: A jolly 'old fellow in the last war

parts.note: a Jolly is old naval slang for a Royal Marine, abbreviated RM
old means aged
a don is a fellow of a college

explanation.surface: Someone recalls a cheerful elderly man who served in the most recent war.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jolly' looks like an adjective for the old fellow, but it is a noun: a Royal Marine.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bible's final battle between good and evil is pictured as the war to end all wars.

clue.text: A chemist's reduced charges

parts.note: MPS stands for Member of the Pharmaceutical Society, a qualified chemist

explanation.surface: A pharmacist has cut prices on prescriptions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reduced' signals a shortened word: the word is a clipped form of amperes, units of electric current.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is the abbreviated plural of ampere, the unit of electrical current, so a cut-down name for measures of charge flow.

clue.text: The state 'of this shapeless body!

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims in dismay at how out of shape their body has become.
explanation.definitionFit: Massachusetts is commonly shortened to its first four letters, and a formless lump of matter is also called this.

clue.text: Potter's craft, of course

parts.note: not pottery: Stephen Potter wrote a famous humorous book on winning at games, golf courses included, by dubious psychological ploys

explanation.surface: Naturally, a potter's skill lies in working clay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Potter' suggests a maker of pots; it is the British humorist Stephen Potter, and 'of course' hints at the golf course.
explanation.definitionFit: Stephen Potter's book coined the term for the art of winning by unsettling an opponent without actually cheating.

clue.text: Balder man shows more of it

definitions.text: Balder man shows more of it

indicators.note: the letters show themselves within the words balder man, so the answer is tucked inside them

explanation.surface: A man going bald reveals more skin on his scalp.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does both jobs: the word sits inside 'Balder man', and a balder man does show more skin.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a word for the skin, or its true inner layer, which a bald head exposes.

clue.text: Showing less than full support for Silver, say

definitions.text: Showing less than full support for Silver, say

parts.words: Showing less than full support for Silver, say
parts.note: Long John Silver, the pirate in Treasure Island, stood on only one leg and a crutch

explanation.surface: Someone gives only lukewarm backing to a candidate called Silver.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Support' reads as backing for a person; it means the legs that hold a body up.
explanation.definitionFit: Long John Silver had lost a leg, so he stood on just one of his two natural supports.

clue.text: Dark blue English flower.

parts.note: a flower here is something that flows, a river; dark blue is the colour of Oxford University, and the Thames at Oxford has its own name

explanation.surface: A deep blue bloom native to England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower' means a river, a thing that flows. Dark blue is Oxford's sporting colour, and Oxford's stretch of the Thames goes by this name.
explanation.definitionFit: The Thames is known by this name as it passes through Oxford, whose university colour is dark blue.

clue.text: Pretty early days for exchanging rings

definitions.text: Pretty early days for exchanging rings

parts.words: Pretty early days for exchanging rings
parts.note: echoes the Shakespeare song calling the start of the year the only pretty ring time, when lovers trade wedding rings

explanation.surface: Someone says it is rather too soon to swap wedding bands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pretty early days' sounds like 'rather too soon'; it is the season at the start of the year, which the song in As You Like It calls 'the only pretty ring time'.
explanation.definitionFit: The season of new growth comes early in the year and is traditionally the time for weddings and love.

clue.text: Such a budget violates one's rights

indicators.note: violates suggests the words one's rights are knocked about and broken up into a new order

explanation.surface: A tight spending plan tramples on people's entitlements.
explanation.walkthrough: 'violates' is the anagram signal for ONE'S RIGHTS.
explanation.definitionFit: A budget run on very little money is described with this word for a bootlace.

clue.text: Late opening in the theatre'

parts.note: the late here are the dead, and the theatre is an operating theatre where a body is opened up

explanation.surface: A show premieres late at night in a playhouse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Late' looks like 'after hours' and 'theatre' like a playhouse; they mean the deceased and the room where a body is examined.
explanation.definitionFit: An examination of a corpse to find the cause of death involves cutting the body open.

clue.text: Work unit: requires oxygen, therefore

parts.note: the erg is a unit of work or energy in physics
O is the chemical symbol for oxygen

explanation.surface: A physics lesson: a unit of work needs oxygen, therefore something follows.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin word for 'so' or 'consequently' is used in English logic.

clue.text: Carter, for example, in digs close to Carnarvon

definitions.text: Carter, for example, in digs close to Carnarvon

parts.words: Carter, for example, in digs close to Carnarvon
parts.note: Howard Carter excavated with Lord Carnarvon, the backer of the Tutankhamun dig; digs are excavations, not lodgings

explanation.surface: A man called Carter is lodging near the Welsh town of Carnarvon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Digs' reads as lodgings and Carnarvon as the Welsh town; Howard Carter found Tutankhamun's tomb with his patron Lord Carnarvon.
explanation.definitionFit: Howard Carter was a scholar of ancient Nile civilisation who excavated pharaohs' tombs.

clue.text: What these salesmen often produce is semi-circular

definitions.text: What these salesmen often produce is semi-circular

parts.words: What these salesmen often produce is semi-circular
parts.note: a circular is a printed leaflet, and a semi is a semi-detached house, the stock of property sellers

explanation.surface: Some salesmen's product tends to be shaped like half a circle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Semi-circular' looks like a shape; split it as a circular (a sales leaflet) advertising a semi (a house joined to its neighbour on one side, common in Britain).
explanation.definitionFit: These people sell houses, and their leaflets often advertise semi-detached homes.

clue.text: Sixth note to get busted main repaired

indicators.note: repaired implies the broken words busted main are put back together in a different arrangement

explanation.surface: A musical sixth note is to be mended after the main part broke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'busted' looks like the anagram signal but is part of the fodder; 'repaired' rearranges BUSTED MAIN.
explanation.definitionFit: In music theory, the sixth degree of a major or minor scale has this technical name.

clue.text: Door-plate stained by. some members of family

definitions.text: Door-plate stained by. some members of family

parts.words: Door-plate stained by. some members of family
parts.note: the same word names a keyhole cover and a family's coat of arms, which disgraceful relatives are said to blot

explanation.surface: Relatives have left marks on the metal plate of a door.
explanation.walkthrough: A door-plate round a keyhole has this name, and so does the shield of family arms; a disgrace is called 'a blot on the family' one.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a keyhole's protective plate and a heraldic shield bearing a family's arms.

clue.text: Not close- sun coming out, diminishing little by little

indicators.note: coming out suggests the word sun breaking loose and reshaping itself

parts.note: paring is cutting something away in thin slices, reducing it bit by bit

explanation.surface: The weather is cool as the sun emerges, then gradually fades.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coming out' rearranges SUN to UNS. 'Close' here means mean with money, not near.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who is close is stingy, so not close means lavish and generous, holding nothing back.

clue.text: There is no system in this sort of chemistry:

definitions.text: There is no system in this sort of chemistry

parts.words: There is no system in this sort of chemistry
parts.note: split the word as in, no organ: an organ is a bodily system, so this chemistry has none, being about non-living compounds

explanation.surface: This branch of chemistry is completely disorganised.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No system' suggests chaos; it means no organ, a bodily system, since this branch studies compounds not derived from living things.
explanation.definitionFit: The branch of chemistry dealing with minerals and compounds lacking carbon chains, not from living organisms.

clue.text: Safe in a prison' cell

explanation.surface: Someone feels secure locked up in jail.
explanation.definitionFit: Old criminal slang uses this word both for a strongbox cracked by safe-blowers and for a cell in a jail.

clue.text: Bruises from these scrimmages

explanation.surface: A rugby player picks up bruises from the scrums.
explanation.definitionFit: To batter someone roughly, and in rugby, loose struggles for the ball held off the ground.

clue.text: Having mod D-banjo tuned, he will accept casual engagements

indicators.note: tuned suggests the strings, here the letters of mod D-banjo, are adjusted into a new order

explanation.surface: A musician with a trendy banjo in D takes on occasional gigs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tuned' rearranges MOD D-BANJO. 'Engagements' sounds like musical gigs, but means bits of casual work.
explanation.definitionFit: A handyman takes on small miscellaneous tasks as and when they come.

clue.text: Tiresome old Dutch dipper?

parts.note: my old Dutch is Cockney rhyming slang for a wife; a tiresome, nagging one was once punished by being plunged in a pond

explanation.surface: A dreary elderly Dutch person goes swimming.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dutch' looks like the nationality; in Cockney rhyming slang 'old Dutch' (Duchess of Fife) is a wife. Nagging wives were punished by being dipped in water from a chair on a beam.
explanation.definitionFit: A chair on a pivoting beam was used to plunge scolds and nagging women into a pond as punishment.

clue.text: Hearing test

explanation.definitionFit: A court hearing of a case is this, and so is an experiment to try something out.

clue.text: Two sporting spectacles

explanation.surface: Two impressive sports events.
explanation.definitionFit: This word means a couple; in cricket, out for nothing in both innings is called a pair of spectacles, from the two zeros.

clue.text: Go to Miss Darling — she's cut off.

indicators.note: cut off says the name loses its tail, the last letter being chopped away

parts.note: Wendy Darling is the girl in J. M. Barrie's Peter Pan

explanation.surface: Visit Miss Darling, who has been isolated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut off' removes the final Y from WENDY.
explanation.definitionFit: To proceed on one's way, as in making one's way home, is an old verb for travel.

clue.text: With cargo left behind in port

indicators.note: behind tells us the letter for left is left behind, dropped from the word

parts.note: a ship with cargo is laden, loaded with goods

explanation.surface: A ship heavy with goods left something behind in harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'left behind' reads as one phrase; split it so 'left' gives L and 'behind' leaves it out of LADEN.
explanation.definitionFit: A harbour city in Yemen at the mouth of the Red Sea was a major coaling port.

clue.text: It will yield a pittance, I expect

indicators.note: will yield suggests the words a pittance, I give up a new word formed from their letters

explanation.surface: Someone resignedly predicts that a venture will pay only a tiny sum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'will yield' rearranges A PITTANCE I.
explanation.definitionFit: To foresee or look forward to something likely to happen is a synonym of expect.

clue.text: Be inclined to vote Democrat

parts.note: a vote is marked with a cross, X, which is the Roman numeral for ten

explanation.surface: Someone leans towards supporting the Democratic party at the polls.
explanation.walkthrough: A voter's cross X doubles as the Roman numeral for ten.
explanation.definitionFit: To have a leaning or a disposition towards something is a synonym phrase.

clue.text: Released a figure from the block in relief

definitions.text: Released a figure from the block in relief

parts.words: Released a figure from the block in relief
parts.note: the block is stone or wood, not an execution block, and relief is carving that stands out, not comfort

explanation.surface: Someone was freed from the scaffold, to the crowd's relief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Block' and 'relief' suggest a reprieved prisoner; they mean a lump of stone and raised carving, as a carver frees a shape from it.
explanation.definitionFit: Carved into shape, as a figure is cut out of stone or wood by an artist.
